title: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
summary: Defines STUN, a tool other protocols use to deal with NAT traversal. An endpoint can use it to learn the address and port a NAT gave it, check connectivity with another endpoint, and keep NAT bindings alive. On its own it is not a complete NAT traversal solution. It obsoletes RFC 3489 and was later replaced by RFC 8489.

plainLanguage.summary: STUN lets a device ask a server which public address and port its network assigned. Other protocols use that information as one part of connecting devices through network address translators.

subtitle: A protocol that helps larger NAT-traversal systems learn the address a network assigns to an endpoint.

tldr.problem: An endpoint behind a Network Address Translator may not know the public address and port that other endpoints see. The earlier STUN specification tried to solve NAT traversal by itself, but the RFC says that approach was not reliable enough.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a Binding request to a STUN server. The server returns the request's observed source address and port in an XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS attribute; other protocols choose when and how to use STUN.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5389 defines STUN as a tool for larger NAT-traversal solutions and obsoletes RFC 3489. RFC 5389 has since been obsoleted by RFC 8489 and updated by RFCs 7350 and 8553.

sections.title: STUN Is a Tool, Not a Complete Solution
sections.content:
Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) lets an endpoint learn the address and port that a Network Address Translator (NAT) assigns to it. It can also help check connectivity and keep a NAT mapping active.

RFC 5389 changes the role of STUN. The previous specification treated STUN as a complete way through NATs, but experience showed that its address results did not always work with peers. This RFC makes STUN a component used by a larger solution, called a STUN usage.
sections.plainLanguage: STUN helps a device learn the address its network shows to other devices. A larger protocol must decide how to use that information to make a connection.

sections.title: A Binding Request Reveals the Mapped Address
sections.content:
In a Binding transaction, a client sends a request to a server. A NAT may change the request's source address and port on its way to the server. The server copies the address it observed into the response's XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS attribute.

The NAT changes the response packet's destination address, but it does not change the address stored inside that attribute. The client can therefore learn its reflexive transport address as seen from the server's side. A Binding indication has no response; receiving one can refresh NAT bindings.

STUN supports UDP, TCP, and TLS over TCP. For UDP requests, the client retransmits after increasing intervals; indications are not retransmitted. The usage defines the transport and any optional procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The server reports the source address it sees on the request. The client reads that address from the reply, while the surrounding protocol decides what to do next.

sections.title: The Header and Its Attributes
sections.content:
Every STUN message begins with a 20-byte header and may contain attributes after it. The header identifies the message type, its length, a fixed magic cookie, and a 96-bit transaction ID. The ID lets a client match a response to its request.

Attributes use a type, length, and value format and end on a 32-bit boundary. An agent may ignore an unfamiliar comprehension-optional attribute. It cannot successfully process a message with an unfamiliar comprehension-required attribute. The fixed header fields and optional FINGERPRINT help distinguish STUN from other protocols sharing a transport address.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a fixed header that identifies its purpose and connects a reply to a request. Extra attributes carry information such as the mapped address or an error.

sections.title: Optional Credentials and Integrity Checks
sections.content:
A STUN usage may select short-term credentials, long-term credentials, or no authentication. With short-term credentials, the client and server obtain a temporary username and password through another protocol. STUN includes the username and a message-integrity value, but never sends the password.

Long-term credentials use a server challenge containing a realm and nonce. The client retries with those values and a message-integrity check. This mechanism cannot protect indications because they receive no response that could challenge the sender. The RFC warns that long-term credentials can be vulnerable to offline password guessing.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol using STUN can require a secret-based check to show that a message is authentic and unchanged. The protocol must choose the credential method; STUN does not require one for every use.

fields.name: Message type
fields.desc: Encodes the method and message class.

fields.name: Message length
fields.desc: Length of the bytes after this header.

fields.name: Magic cookie
fields.desc: Fixed value used to identify STUN.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.desc: Identifies the transaction and matches its response.
